en: The Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna, in one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
As the Bhagavān briefly taught the five aggregates:
first, the aggregate of form; second, the aggregate of feeling; third, the aggregate of perception; fourth, the aggregate of formations; and fifth, the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of form?
It refers to the four great elements and the various forms derived from the four great elements.
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What is the earth element?
It is the quality of solidity and rigidity.
What is the water element?
It is the nature of flowing and moisture.
What is the fire element?
That is to say, it has the nature of warmth and dryness.
What is the wind element?
It is the nature of lightness and mobility.
What are the various forms derived from the four great elements?

They are the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty; visible form, sound, odor, taste, a portion of the tangible, and non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), and so forth.
What is the eye faculty?
It is the translucent matter that has visible form as its object.
What is the ear faculty?
That is to say, it is the translucent matter that has sound as its object.
What is the nose faculty?
It is the translucent matter that has odor as its object.
What is the tongue faculty?
It is the translucent matter that has taste as its object.
What is the body faculty?
It refers to pure matter that has the tangible as its object.
What is matter? It refers to the objective domain of the eye, namely, manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), and informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).

What is sound? It refers to the objective domain of the ear: sound caused by appropriated great elements, sound caused by non-appropriated great elements, and sound caused by both types of great elements.
What is odor? It refers to the objective domain of the nose: pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and all other remaining odors. What is taste?
This refers to the objects of the tongue: sweet taste, sour taste, salty taste, pungent taste, bitter taste, and bland taste.
What is meant by "a portion of the tangible"?

This refers to the objective domain of the body, consisting of derived tangible objects other than the four great elements, such as smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
What is meant by "non-informative matter" (avijñapti-rūpa) and so forth?
It refers to matter produced by informative action (vijñapti-karman) and meditative concentration (samādhi), which is invisible and non-obstructive.
What is the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha)?
That is to say, there are three types of experience:
first, suffering; second, pleasure; and third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Pleasure is defined as that which gives rise to a desire for union at the time of its cessation.
Suffering refers to the desire for separation that exists at the time of birth;
neither-suffering-nor-pleasure refers to the absence of both desires.
What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
This refers to grasping various characteristics within objects.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?
It refers to all other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), excluding feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
What are called the other mental factors?
They are those phenomena that are associated with the mind. What, then, are they?
They are: contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition;
desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
faith, shame, dread, the wholesome root of non-attachment, the wholesome root of non-hatred, the wholesome root of non-delusion, diligence, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming.
Greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt;

anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, avarice, deceit, guile, arrogance, and harmfulness; lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension;
regret, sleep, applied thought, and sustained thought.
Regarding these mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*):

five are universal (*sarvatraga*), five are object-specific (*viniyata*), eleven are wholesome (*kuśala*), six are afflictions (*kleśa*), the remainder are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four are indeterminate (*aniyata*).
What is contact?
It has the nature of the discernment resulting from the coming together of the three.
What is attention?
It has the nature of being able to cause the mind to awaken.
What is volition (*cetanā*)?
It has the nature of mental action (*manas-karma*) that causes the mind to engage in the performance of actions regarding virtues, faults, and that which is neither.
What is desire (*chanda*)?
It is characterized by the aspiration for agreeable objects.
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
It refers to having the nature of confirming a determined object exactly as it has been understood.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
It refers to having the nature of causing the mind not to forget and clearly recording an object with which one is familiar.
What is samādhi? It is characterized by causing the mind to remain one-pointed upon the object of observation without distraction.
What is wisdom (prajñā)?
It refers to that which has the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) as its intrinsic nature;
it is either induced by correct reasoning, induced by incorrect reasoning, or induced by neither.
What is faith (*śraddhā*)?
It is defined as having the nature of a pure mind that is perfectly in accord with karma, its results, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels.
What is *hrī* (shame)?
It is defined as having the nature of feeling shame regarding committed transgressions, based on oneself and based on the Dharma.
What is shame (*hrī*)?
It is characterized by the predominance of the world (*loka-adhipati*), having the nature of feeling ashamed of the transgressions one has committed.
What is non-attachment (*alobha*)?
It refers to the antidote to greed, having the nature of profound revulsion and non-attachment.
What is non-hatred?
It refers to the antidote to hatred, having loving-kindness as its nature.
What is non-delusion?
It is the antidote to delusion, having as its nature correct practice in accordance with reality.
What is diligence?
It refers to the antidote to laziness; its nature is the mind’s courageous vigor toward wholesome qualities.
What is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)?
It refers to the antidote to coarseness and heaviness (*dausthulya*); its nature is the physical and mental composure, flexibility, and capability [for practice].
What is non-negligence?
It is the antidote to negligence, namely, from non-attachment up to diligence.
By relying upon these, one abandons unwholesome dharmas and cultivates their wholesome antidotes.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It refers to non-attachment and so forth, up to diligence.
By relying upon these, one attains all forms of mental evenness, mental rectitude, and mental unperturbedness.
Furthermore, because of this, one dwells without defilement amidst those defiled phenomena that have already been eliminated.
What is non-harming?
It refers to the antidote to harming, having compassion as its essential nature.
What is greed? It is characterized by the nature of stained affection and attachment toward the five aggregates of clinging.
What is hatred?
It is characterized by the tendency to take pleasure in harming sentient beings.
What is pride? It refers to the seven types of pride:

1. Pride (māna), 2. Excessive pride (atimāna), 3. Pride beyond pride (mānātimāna), 4. The pride of "I am" (asmimāna), 5. Arrogant pride (abhimāna), 6. Inferiority pride (ūnamāna), and 7. False pride (mithyāmāna).
What is pride (*māna*)?
It is defined as the nature of mental loftiness, consisting in considering oneself superior to those who are inferior, or considering oneself equal to those who are equal.
What is excessive pride (*atimāna*)?
It is characterized by the mind’s inflation when one considers oneself superior to those who are equal, or considers oneself equal to those who are superior.
What is pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*)?
It is characterized by the mind’s inflation when one considers oneself superior to those who are actually superior.
What is the conceit of self (*asmimāna*)?
It is the nature of the mind being uplifted by viewing the five aggregates of clinging as "I" or "mine.
What is overweening conceit (*adhimāna*)?
It is defined as the nature of mental inflation, wherein one claims to have attained a superior and distinguished realization that has not yet been attained.
What is inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*)?
It is defined as the nature of mental inflation based on the thought that one is only slightly inferior when compared to those who are largely superior.
What is false pride (*mithyāmāna*)?
It is the nature of the mind being uplifted by conceiving oneself to possess virtues when one actually lacks them.
What is ignorance (*avidyā*)?
It is defined as having the nature of ignorance regarding karma and its results, as well as the Truths and the Jewels.
This, moreover, is of two kinds: that which is innate and that which arises from discrimination.

Furthermore, the greed, hatred, and ignorance bound to the desire realm are called the three unwholesome roots: namely, the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
What are the views? They are the so-called five views:

first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and fifth, the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
What is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
It is the defiled wisdom that regards the five aggregates of clinging as either a self or as belonging to a self.
What is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
That is to say, by the very power of that [view], it regards things as either eternal or as subject to annihilation; its nature is defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*).
What is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
It refers to either the denial of cause or the denial of result, or the denial of efficacy, or the subversion of wholesome phenomena; its nature is defiled wisdom.
What is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?
It is the defiled wisdom that regards those three views, as well as the aggregates upon which they depend, as supreme, foremost, excellent, and ultimate. Its nature is defiled wisdom.
What is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
It is the nature of defiled wisdom that regards rules, observances, and the aggregates upon which they depend as being purification, liberation, and transcendence.
What is doubt? It is characterized by hesitation regarding the truths and so forth.
Among the afflictions, the last three views and doubt arise solely from discrimination; the remaining ones pertain to both innate and discriminative arising.
What is anger (*krodha*)?
It is characterized by the nature of mental affliction and distress when encountering present circumstances that are disadvantageous.
What is resentment (*upanāha*)?
It has the nature of not relinquishing a grudge.
What is concealment (*mrakṣa*)?
It has the nature of hiding one's own transgressions.
What is vexation (*pradāśa*)?
It is characterized by the nature of uttering violent and malicious speech with persistent resentment.
What is envy (*īrṣyā*)?
It is defined as having the nature of envy toward the prosperity of others.
What is stinginess?
It is defined as having the nature of a mind of parsimony that is contrary to giving.
What is deception (*māyā*)?
It is characterized by the fraudulent manifestation of unreal things for the purpose of deceiving others.
What is guile (*śāṭhya*)?
What is called *mrakṣa* (concealment) has as its nature a crookedness of mind comprised by the means of hiding one's own faults.
What is *mada* (intoxication/arrogance)?
It has as its nature a haughty mind that relies upon and is attached to one's own flourishing prosperity.
What is harm? It has the nature of causing injury and affliction to sentient beings.
What is lack of shame?
It is defined as having the nature of not feeling shame for one's committed transgressions with respect to oneself.
What is "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*)?
It is defined as having the nature of not feeling shame for one's committed transgressions with respect to others.
What is lethargy (*styāna*)?
It is characterized by the mind being unrefined, lacking capability, and being dull-witted.
What is restlessness (*auddhatya*)?
It is characterized by a lack of mental tranquility. What is non-faith?
It is that which is the antithesis of faith;
it is characterized by a lack of correct conviction and compliance regarding karma, its results, and so forth, and by a lack of purity of mind.
What is laziness (*kausīdya*)?
It is that which is the antithesis of diligence (*vīrya*); its nature is the lack of vigor in the mind regarding all categories of the wholesome.
What is negligence (*pramāda*)?

It refers to that which, by reason of greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness, has as its nature the failure to guard the mind against various afflictions and the inability to cultivate various categories of wholesome qualities.
What is loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*)?
It refers to defiled mindfulness, which has as its nature the inability to clearly remember various wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*).
What is distraction (*vikṣepa*)?
It is defined as having the nature of the mind wandering due to the influence of greed, hatred, and delusion.
What is non-discernment (*asamprajanya*)?
It is defined as having the nature of not abiding correctly within the present activity of body, speech, and mind.
What is remorse? It has the nature of mental regret. What is sleep?
It is defined as having the nature of a mind that functions without mastery and is extremely dull and brief.
What is vitarka?
It is defined as having the nature of a coarse state of mind, consisting of a specific form of investigation through mental verbalization, which is a distinction of volition and wisdom.
What is investigation (*vicāra*)?
It is defined as having the nature of causing the mind to become subtle through the specific distinctions of mental verbalization, conceptual discrimination, volition, and wisdom.
What are the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)?

This refers to that which is provisionally established based on the states of form, mind, and mental factors; it cannot be designated as having a definitive nature of difference or non-difference. What, then, is it?

These refer to such categories as acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the commonality of group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the body of names (*nāma-kāya*), the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), the body of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), and the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
What is meant by "attainment"?
It refers to either acquisition or accomplishment.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, as a seed, as mastery, or as manifest presence, according to what is appropriate.
What is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?

It is defined as the cessation of the mind and mental factors that do not constantly manifest, preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of renunciation, occurring in one who has already abandoned craving for the Sphere of Total Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) but has not yet abandoned craving for the higher realms.
What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

It is defined as having already abandoned craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), seeking further progress beyond the first dhyāna, and being characterized by the cessation of the constant activity and a portion of the constantly active mind and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention to the perception of cessation.
What is the nature of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*)?
It refers to the fruit of the meditative attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Its essential nature consists in the cessation of the mind and mental factors that do not constantly manifest once one has been born among the gods of the Non-conceptualizing Sentient Beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*).
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It is that which, within a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), is projected by prior karma and has the nature of determining the duration of existence.
What is a homogeneous class of beings?
It refers to the nature of sentient beings being similar to their own kind.
What is birth? It refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) being present where they were previously non-existent.
What is aging? It is characterized by the nature of the transformation within the continuity of these very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). What is duration?
That is to say, its nature is the continuous succession and evolution of these very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
How is it impermanent?
Its nature is the cessation and disappearance of the continuity of these very conditioned phenomena.
What is the "body of names" (nāmakāya)?
It has as its nature the metaphorical designation for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
What is the "body of phrases" (padakāya)?
It has as its nature the designations for the distinctions among all phenomena.
What is the "body of syllables" (*vyañjana-kāya*)?
It has as its nature the individual letters (*akṣara*), because they are able to manifest the former two kinds [of bodies].
It is also called "manifestation" (*vyañjana*), because it serves as the basis for names and phrases to manifest meaning;
it is also called "syllable" (*akṣara*), because it is not subject to alteration by means of differentiation.
What is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is defined as the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Such categories as these have already been explained under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
It has the nature of discerning its respective objects.
It is also called mind (*citta*) and mentation (*manas*), because it accumulates [impressions] and because it is subsumed under mentation.
The "supreme mind" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*. Why is this?
Because within this consciousness, the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are gathered and accumulated.
Furthermore, this functioning based on objects cannot be differentiated; it proceeds as a continuous stream of a single type from beginning to end.

Moreover, because of this, when one emerges from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), or the state of non-conception itself, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that discern objects arise once again. This is because they evolve in dependence upon specific objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*), because they repeatedly interrupt and then resume their activity, and because they cause the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to flow on and revolve.

The ālayavijñāna is so called because it can store and conceal all seeds, because it can store and conceal the manifestation of the conceit "I am," and because it takes the body as its objective support.
This very consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna*, because it is able to grasp and maintain the body.

As for the "supreme manas," this refers to the consciousness that takes the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its object and is constantly associated with self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*). It continues to evolve as a homogeneous stream from one moment to the next, except during the state of the fruit of Arhatship, when the Noble Path is present, and when the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is manifest.
Question:
"For what reason is it called a 'skandha'? Answer:
"They are called aggregates (*skandha*) in the sense of accumulation;
that is to say, because they comprise a concise synthesis of the various categories of form and so forth, distinguished by their continuity in the world, their types, and their spheres of engagement.

Furthermore, there are twelve bases (*āyatana*): the eye-base and the form-base, the ear-base and the sound-base, the nose-base and the odor-base, the tongue-base and the taste-base, the body-base and the tangible-base, and the mind-base and the mental-object-base.
The five bases beginning with the eye, as well as the bases of visible form, sound, odor, and taste, have already been explained as before.
As for the term "base of the tangible" (spraṣṭavyāyatana), it refers to the four great elements (mahābhūta) and a portion of the tangible objects previously mentioned.
What is called the sense-field of mind (*manāyatana*) is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

What is called the sense-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāraskandhas*), as well as unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the unconditioned?
These refer to the unconditioned space, the unconditioned cessation not through deliberation, the unconditioned cessation through deliberation, and suchness, among others. What is space?
It is that which accommodates all forms.
What is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
It refers to a cessation that is not dissociation (*visaṃyoga*). What, then, is this?
It refers to the ultimate non-arising of the aggregates in the absence of the antidote to the afflictions.
What is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? It is that cessation which is dissociation (*visamyoga*).
What, then, is this? It refers to the ultimate non-arising of the aggregates due to the application of the antidotes to the afflictions. What is suchness?
It refers to the dharma-nature of all phenomena and the selflessness of phenomena.
Question:
"For what reason is it called a 'basis' (āyatana)?"
Answer: "The meaning of being a gateway for the growth and arising of the various consciousnesses is the meaning of 'base' (*āyatana*).

Furthermore, there are the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
The various elements of the eye and so forth, as well as the various elements of form and so forth, are as explained in the section on the bases (*āyatana*).
As for the six consciousness elements, their nature is the discernment [of objects] based upon the faculties of the eye and so forth, and with respect to the objects of form and so forth.

As for what is called the "mind-element" (manodhātu), it refers to that which has just ceased without interval and so forth; this is intended to indicate the sixth consciousness and to establish the eighteen elements in detail.

Thus, the aggregate of form consists of ten bases, ten elements, and a portion of the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*); the aggregate of consciousness consists of the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the seven mind elements; and the remaining three aggregates, a portion of the aggregate of form, and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute the base of mental objects and the element of mental objects.
Question: For what reason is it called a "constituent" (*dhātu*)?
Answer: It is called a "constituent" because it has the sense of being able to maintain its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is devoid of functional activity (*nirvyāpāra*).
Question:
"For what purpose are the aggregates (skandha) and so forth taught? Answer:
"In order to counteract the three types of self-grasping, there are, respectively, these three types of self-grasping:
namely, grasping at a unitary self, grasping at a self as an experiencer, and grasping at a self as an agent."
Furthermore, among these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many possess form?
They are ten elements and a portion of one, namely the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
How many are formless?
This refers to the remaining elements.
How many are visible?
Only one: the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
How many are non-visible?
They are the remaining elements.
How many are resistant?
This refers to the ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*).
If these are obstructed within a given location, this constitutes the meaning of "having resistance" (*sapratigha*).
How many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
This refers to the remaining elements (*dhātu*).
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
They are fifteen elements and a portion of the final three, because afflictions arise in these locations and because they are the spheres where [afflictions] currently operate.
How many are untainted (*anāsrava*)?
They are a portion of the last three.
How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
That is to say, all of them.
How many are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
Fourteen; that is to say, excluding odor, taste, and the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses.
How many are bound to the formless realm?
They are the last three.
How many are unbound?
That is to say, this very untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu).
By how many aggregates (skandha) is it subsumed?
It is subsumed by all except for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
How many are comprised within the aggregates of clinging?
Those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
How many are wholesome (*kuśala*)?
How many are unwholesome?
How many are indeterminate?
It is said that ten are of all three types; the seven mind-elements, as well as the elements of visible form, sound, and mental objects, are eightfold and indeterminate.
How many are internal?
They are twelve, excluding the elements of visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*).
How many are external?
That is to say, six [elements] are those to be excluded.
How many have objects?
They are the seven mind-elements and a portion of the dharma-element consisting of mental factors.
How many are without an object?
They are the remaining ten [elements] and a portion of the dharma-element.
How many possess conceptual discrimination?
This refers to the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and a portion of the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*).
How many are appropriated (*upātta*)?
They are the five internal elements and a portion of four other elements, namely: visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
How many are non-appropriated?
They are the remaining nine and a portion of the four.
How many are of the same class (sabhāga)?
This refers to the five internal bases possessing form, because they share the same objects as their respective consciousnesses.
How many of these are "homogeneous" (sabhāga)?
It refers to those very same [bases] when their respective consciousnesses are absent, because they remain equal to their own kind.
The Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna, in one fascicle.
